newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ABARE cuts Australia commodity growth f'cast.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ABARE cuts Australia commodity growth f'cast.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) has reduced its forecast of Australian commodity export growth in 1997/98 to 3.9 percent due to the prospect of drier than normal weather.

The lower growth forecast, which puts Australia's forecast total commodity exports in 1997/98 at a record A$60.76 billion, is down from ABARE's previous forecast of 7.3 percent growth for 1997/98 to June 30 because of reduced expected farm production.

The forecast 3.9 percent growth, contained in ABARE's June quarter commodities report, is up from estimated growth of 2.6 percent in 1996/97, when Australia is expected to export a total A$58.5 billion worth of commodities.
The biggest single cut in ABARE's 1997/98 forecast is in wheat, where ABARE has reduced its production forecast to 16.25 million tonnes from its previous forecast 19.2 million tonnes.

"Prospects of drier than normal seasonal conditions, as a result of a developing El Nino weather pattern, will contribute to a forecast five percent fall in the value of farm exports to A$20.2 billion in 1997/98," Stephen Beare, ABARE's acting executive director, said in a statement.
But a strong export performance by the minerals and energy sector would see the total value Australian commodities exports rising in 1997/98.
Mineral resource exports are forecast to rise by nine percent to A$38.2 billion, with world prices for most metals forecast to rise over the remainder of 1997 and in 1998.

In its last quarterly forecast, issued on March 18, ABARE forecast Australia's total 1997/98 commodity exports would grow by 7.3 percent to A$62.43 billion. The value of farm exports was forecast to rise by 2.8 percent, while exports of mineral resource commodities were forecast to rise by 9.9 percent.

ABARE forecasts aggregate unit returns for exports of Australian commodities will rise by 1.6 percent in 1997/98, with a three percent overall improvement in mineral exports expected to be partly offset by a 1.2 percent decline in farm returns.
"Lower winter crop production, and hence lower exports of grains, is a major factor in the forecast fall in farm exports," Beare said.

Crop yields are forecast to be below average in Australia's eastern states, reflecting the Bureau of Meteorology's announcement that it is confident an El Nino weather pattern will persist for the remainder of the year, he said.
With yields well below last season's record, the wheat crop is forecast to be down about 30 percent to 16.2 million tonnes, despite plantings being little changed, he said.

ABARE's wheat crop forecast, down from the 19.2 million tonnes forecast in its June 3 Australian Crop Report, is also less than the the 17.82 million tonnes predicted in its March 18 Australian Commodities quarterly forecast.

Reflecting weather related problems in North America and Europe, as well as in Australia, the world indicator price for wheat is forecast to average slightly higher in 1997/98 at US$185.00 a tonne, ABARE said on Tuesday.
With some demand improvement, the eastern market indicator for wool is forecast to average six percent higher in 1997/98.
Australian cattle saleyard prices are forecast to rise an average nine percent as U.S. and North Asian demand strengthens.

If dry conditions persist, poor pasture conditions in parts of New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia can be expected to deteriorate further. In that event there could be a rise in forced yardings of cattle and sheep, with a corresponding adverse effect on livestock prices, Beare said.
ABARE also forecast significantly higher prices in 1998 for aluminium, up eight percent, nickel, up 15 percent, zinc, up 12 percent and crude oil, up seven percent.
